newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Mauritius businesses need skilled labour.
newsitem.headline: Mauritius businesses need skilled labour.

text.p: Mauritius needs more highly skilled labour as it modernises its economy and makes increased use of advanced technology, the Mauritius Employers' Federation (MEF) said on Monday.

"Machines have replaced human beings in several areas. This has increased the volume of work and requires more labour, but qualified labour only. We are now evolving in a more complex world," Director Azad Jeetun told Reuters.
The need for skilled workers is the result of an economic boom in the second half of the 1980s in Mauritius.

The boom was spearheaded by the textiles-led Export Processing Zone (EPZ) which used low-skilled, cheap but educated labour. It succeeded in wiping out unemployment by 1987 and became the biggest sectoral employer in the island.
But as labour ran short, wage increases outstripped productivity until textile exports were no longer competitive internationally, economists said.
In addition the foundation of the World Trade Organisation meant Mauritian exporters had to increase productivity and increase quality by modernising their manufacturing.
"Many Mauritian enterprises have restructured themselves and invested heavily in information technology and automation," Jeetun said.

In 1991, employment in the EPZ reached an all-time high of 90,900 in 586 factories. But as factories modernised and those failing to do so closed down, EPZ employment fell. The latest figures showed 79,300 employed in 475 factories by June 1996.
But job creation is still seen on the cards for the EPZ.
A recent MEF survey showed it would account for 56 percent of the 5,100 jobs expected to be created by the private sector in the financial year ending 30 June 1997.

"Job losses will in future be concentrated among the unskilled whereas most jobs of the future will belong to those with good education and skills. There is a need for well-focused and high-level training not only at professional but also at technical levels," the MEF survey report said.

MEF's director Jeetun estimates some 2,000 extra jobs will be created in the small and medium enterprises in 1996/97. But this will not be enough to absorb the 10,000 school leavers expected to join the job market in the same period.
"Growth imperatively needs to be at least six percent to create employment (to absorb all 10,000 new workers)," he said.
Economic growth in Mauritius was 5.7 percent in 1996, up from 5.3 percent in 1995.
